WD-2: I can select necessary columns from a dataset.

Example selecting specified columns

{r}
#| label: wd-2-ex-1

# Lab 4 Question 7 - selecting specific columns for pivoting
ca_childcare |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(mc_infant, mc_toddler, mc_preschool),  # selecting columns
    names_to = "age_group",
    values_to = "price"
  )

Example removing specified columns

{r}
#| label: wd-2-ex-2

# Lab 3 Question 5 - selecting only necessary columns
teacher_evals_clean <- teacher_data |> 
  select(course_id, teacher_id, question_no, no_participants, 
         resp_share, SET_score_avg, percent_failed_cur, 
         academic_degree, seniority, sex)

Example selecting columns based on logical values (e.g., starts_with(), ends_with(), contains(), where())

{r}
#| label: wd-2-ex-3

# Lab 4 Question 6 - selecting columns that start with "mc_"
ca_childcare_long <- ca_childcare_clean |>
  select(study_year, region, mc_infant, mc_toddler, mc_preschool) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("mc_"), 
               names_to = "age", 
               values_to = "price")

WD-7: I can pivot dataframes from long to wide and visa versa

pivot_longer()

{r}
#| label: wd-7-long

# Lab 4 Question 7 - pivoting from wide to long
ca_childcare |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(mc_infant, mc_toddler, mc_preschool),
    names_to = "age_group",
    values_to = "price"
  )

pivot_wider()

{r}
#| label: wd-7-wide

# Lab 4 Question 5 - pivoting from long to wide
ca_median_income <- ca_childcare |> 
  filter(study_year %in% c(2008, 2018)) |> 
  group_by(census_region, study_year) |>
  summarize(median_income = median(mhi_2018)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = study_year, 
              values_from = median_income)

R-2: I can write well documented and tidy code.

Example of ggplot2 plotting

{r}
#| label: r-2-1

# Lab 4, Question 7

data_plot <- ca_childcare |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(mc_infant, mc_toddler, mc_preschool),
    names_to = "age_group",
    values_to = "price"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    age_group = str_remove(age_group, "mc_"),
    age_group = str_to_title(age_group),
    age_group = fct_relevel(age_group, "Infant", "Toddler", "Preschool")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = study_year, y = price, color = census_region)) + 
  geom_point(size = 0.8) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) + 
  facet_wrap(~ age_group) +
  labs(
    x = "Study Year",
    y = "Weekly Median Price for Center-Based Childcare ($)",
    color = "California Region"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2008, 2018, 2)) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "turbo") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    strip.text = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold")
  )

data_plot

At least one numeric variable and one categorical variable

{r}

# Lab 2, Question 16 - Boxplot with jitter
ggplot(data = surveys,
       aes(x = weight, y = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +

  labs(x = "Body Weight (grams)",

At least two categorical variables

ggplot(teacher_evals_compare, aes(x = sen_level, fill = SET_level)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") + 
  geom_text(
    aes(label = after_stat(count)),

  scale_fill_manual(

  theme_minimal() +

DSSM-2: I can conduct common statistical analyses in R.

Example 1

{r}
#| label: dssm-2-1

# Challenge 3 Question 3 - Chi-square test
chisq.test(teacher_evals_compare$SET_level, 
           teacher_evals_compare$sen_level)

# Results: X-squared = 10.207, df = 2, p-value = 0.006075
# Interpretation: Evaluation level and seniority are not independent (p < 0.05)

Example 2

{r}
#| label: dssm-2-2

# Lab 4 Question 9 - Linear regression
reg_mod1 <- lm(mc_infant ~ mhi_2018, data = ca_childcare)
summary(reg_mod1)

# Interpretation: For each $1 increase in median household income, 
# infant childcare costs increase by $0.002241 (p < 0.001)
# R-squared = 0.635 (63.5% of variance explained)

Example 3

{r}
#| label: dssm-2-3

# Lab 2 Question 17 - ANOVA
species_mod <- aov(weight ~ species, data = surveys)
summary(species_mod)

# Conclusion: At least one species has significantly different 
# mean weight (F = 19916, p < 0.001)

Revising My Thinking

Throughout the first half of the quarter, I have submitted revisions for most of my completed assignments, specifically in those were I felt like there was more for me to learn in. This represents my commitment to learning from feedback, improving my work, and r skills.

Lab 3 Revisions - Key Learnings

Revision 1: Data Description Context

Original Issue: My description only mentioned the structure (rows, columns, data types) without providing important context about where, when, how, and why the data were collected.

What I Learned: Understanding data context is essential for proper analysis and interpretation. I now automatically include who collected the data, when, for what purpose, and under what conditions in all my data descriptions. This deeper understanding helps me make better analytical decisions.

Revision 2: Code Formatting

Original Issue: My code line was too long (over 80 characters).

What I Changed: Added line breaks after pipes and commas to keep lines under 80 characters.

What I Learned: Code should have line breaks after pipes and commas for readability. I now automatically format my code properly in new assignments, making it more readable and professional. Good formatting isn't just aesthetic—it makes debugging easier and helps collaborators understand my work.

Revision 3: Function Syntax

Original Issue: I wasn't using explicit, named arguments in functions like if_any().

What I Changed: Updated to use .cols and .fns as named arguments with formula syntax ~ is.na(.x).

What I Learned: The if_any() function takes .cols and .fns as named arguments. Using formula syntax ~ is more explicit and follows tidyverse conventions. This reflection showed me why certain syntax matters, not just what is correct. Understanding the reasoning helps me make better decisions in future coding and recognize similar patterns in other functions.

Challenge 3 Revisions - Key Learnings

Revision 1: Visualization Labels

Original Issue: My plot was missing percentage labels that would make it easier to interpret.

What I Changed: Added geom_text() with position_fill() to display counts on the bars.

What I Learned: Using geom_text() with position_fill() adds labels. The after_stat() function accesses computed statistics. This taught me that visualizations should be self-explanatory without requiring readers to mentally calculate proportions. Good visualizations do the work for the reader.

Revision 2: Statistical Interpretation

Original Issue: My statistical conclusions lacked context about what the variables actually measured.

What I Changed: Rewrote conclusions to include what variables represent, not just statistical values.

What I Learned: Always provide context about what variables measure in conclusions. A complete conclusion should be self-contained and interpretable on its own. I now ensure my interpretations include what the variables actually mean rather than just citing statistical values. This makes my work accessible to broader audiences.

Revision 3: Document Structure

Original Issue: I was using headers for individual question responses rather than major sections.

What I Changed: Reserved headers for major document sections and used bold text for question numbers.

What I Learned: Headers should be reserved for major document sections, not individual question responses. This improved the overall organization and readability of my documents. Proper document hierarchy helps readers navigate and understand the flow of analysis.

Evidence of Growth

These revisions demonstrate that I understand why changes improve my work, not just what to change. Key evidence of growth:

Application to Future Work: I incorporate lessons learned from revisions into future assignments and rarely repeat the same mistakes. For example, I was improperly formatting my YAML heading and after revisions I have successfully submitted lab 6-8 with correct YAML headers. 

Deeper Understanding: My revision reflections show understanding of underlying principles (e.g., why explicit syntax matters, why context is essential) rather than just surface-level fixes.

Proactive Improvement: In later assignments, I apply these lessons before receiving feedback, showing that I've internalized the improvements.

Cumulative Learning: Each revision builds on previous ones—better formatting leads to more readable code, which makes it easier to spot logical improvements, which leads to better analysis.

Peer Support & Collaboration

Collaborative Group Member

Throughout Practice Activities, I have been patient, respectful, and followed collaborative protocol consistently:

Protocol Adherence: - Strictly switched between Typer and Talker roles as instructed in all activities - As Talker: Always explained my reasoning completely before having partner type. Example: "I think we should use inner_join() here because we only want suspects who match both criteria—the gym membership and the car description." - As Typer: Actively listened and asked clarifying questions rather than just typing what I thought. Example: "So you want to filter before joining? Can you explain why that order is better?" - Respected the learning process by letting my partner work through problems rather than jumping to give answers

Communication Style: - Always explained reasoning before suggesting code: Rather than just saying "use inner_join," I explain: "I think we should use inner_join() here because we only want suspects who match both criteria, and inner_join only keeps rows that appear in both tables." - Asked open-ended questions: Instead of "Should we use inner_join?", I ask "What type of join do you think would work best here and why?" This helps my partner develop their thinking. - Built on partner's ideas: When my partner suggests something, I engage with it: "That's a good idea to filter first! That will make the join faster since we're working with less data." - Listened actively: I repeat back what I hear to confirm understanding: "So you're saying we should group by teacher first, then calculate the average?"

Examples of Good Collaboration: - When my partner was stuck on a join, instead of giving the answer, I asked: "What information do we need from each table? Let's list that out first." - When I disagreed with an approach, I framed it constructively: "I see why you're thinking that way. Have we considered what happens if there are missing values?" - When my partner had a great idea I hadn't thought of, I acknowledged it: "Oh, that's clever! I didn't think to use distinct() there, but that will definitely help."

Areas for Continued Growth: - Patience: Occasionally I get excited about a solution and want to jump ahead—I'm working on being more patient and letting the process unfold naturally - Question depth: Could ask even more probing questions to help partner develop deeper understanding (e.g., "Why do you think that approach would work?" instead of just "What should we do?") - Balance efficiency with learning: Sometimes I focus too much on finishing quickly—need to remember the goal is learning, not just task completion

Overall Assessment: I demonstrate excellent collaboration with consistent protocol adherence, patient and respectful communication, and genuine interest in my partner's learning and ideas. I view collaboration as an opportunity for mutual growth rather than just task completion. My communication style is clear, supportive, and focused on understanding rather than just completing the task.

Peer Code Review

I have provided peer code reviews every week, offering specific, constructive feedback that demonstrates genuine desire to help classmates improve.

Characteristics of My Reviews:

1. Specific and Actionable - Instead of: "Your code could be better" - I write: "On line 23, consider using n_distinct(teacher_id) instead of length(unique(teacher_id))—it's more concise and follows tidyverse style"

2. Explains the "Why" - "Your pipe would be more readable with line breaks after each |> because it keeps each operation visible without horizontal scrolling" - "Using fct_relevel() here would preserve your factor order in the plot, preventing alphabetical sorting"

3. Balances Constructive Criticism with Recognition - "Great use of facet_wrap() here—it makes comparing species really clear!" - "Your comments are helpful, and I especially like how you explained the join logic. One suggestion: consider adding units to your axis labels (e.g., 'Weight (grams)')."

4. Provides Examples When suggesting improvements, I often include a small code snippet showing the alternative approach:

# Instead of multiple mutate() calls, you could combine them:
mutate(var1 = ...,
       var2 = ...)

Example Review (Lab 3):

"Great work on Question 5! I really like your data cleaning pipeline; it's structured well and efficient. I especially like how you used across() to convert multiple columns at once—that's much cleaner than doing them individually. One small suggestion: in Question 10, I think there's a typo in your written answer where you mention "54605" twice (once for highest and once for lowest). The output shows 54605 had the highest score alongside 50746, while only 51356 had the lowest. Just double-check that interpretation!

Your use of multi-step grouping in Questions 10-12 is excellent! One tip for readability: you could round your percentages in the summarise() step using something like avg_resp = round(mean(course_resp, na.rm = TRUE), 3). This would make your output tables cleaner and your written summaries easier to write!

Nice job using if_any(everything(), is.na in Question 8 to find missing values—that's a really elegant solution! One small enhancement for Question 7: instead of just showing counts for academic degrees, you could add mutate(percentage = n/sum(n) * 100) after your count() to show the percentage distribution, which would make comparisons easier to interpret. Overall great work:)"

What Makes This Review Effective: 1. Starts with positive recognition of what works well 2. Provides specific line/question references so student knows exactly where to look 3. Explains why changes would improve the code (readability, efficiency) 4. Gives concrete examples of better syntax 5. Ends encouragingly while summarizing key improvements

Honesty and Kindness: My reviews are honest about areas for improvement while maintaining a supportive, kind tone. I frame suggestions as opportunities for growth rather than criticism. For example: - Not: "Your code is wrong here" - Instead: "This is close! One thing to consider is..."

I believe giving meaningful feedback is part of being a good community member and helps create a supportive learning environment where everyone feels comfortable taking risks and improving.
